paras: The shooting of Manning Law was the pursuit and shooting of a Black man, Manning Law, by the two brothers of his white bride, Mary Lewis, in Lexington County, South Carolina, in late October 1881. Overtaken on the road soon after the wedding, Law fired at the brothers and was shot in the breast; one dispatch said he was killed, while fuller versions said he was mortally wounded and that it was not known whether he died. Papers from Illinois to Tennessee carried the story under headlines about "miscegenation", and one cited it as a case of "Judge Lynch".

Mary Lewis was a white woman living in Lexington County whom the dispatches described as "well connected" and of "a respectable family". According to a Columbia telegraph dated October 28, she married Law "this morning", though other versions put the wedding on a Friday or "Thursday last". The Chicago Tribune said the ceremony was performed "as privately as possible", after which the couple set out by buggy for Augusta, Georgia.

When the woman's two brothers learned of the marriage, they set out after the couple and overtook them "at a point called Buck Creek", or, in the Tribune's telling, about ten miles into the journey. Every account says Law, "apprehending death at the hands of his pursuers", drew a pistol and fired first, and the brothers returned fire. One shot struck Law in the breast, and the Charleston special said the wound "will probably prove fatal".

The brothers then went to the house of the preacher who had married the couple and threatened to kill him. He ran into the woods with the brothers firing after him, hid in a thicket, and reached Columbia by the night train, where he gave his account to a correspondent.

The dispatches built on the preacher's account ended by saying it was not known whether Law had died or what had become of his wife and her brothers. No report of an arrest, inquest or prosecution of the brothers appears in the coverage, and the Tribune closed with them "reloading their pistols".

All of the surviving coverage comes from the white press, and nearly all of it from outside South Carolina, spread by telegraph from Columbia and Charleston between November 2 and 12. The Ottawa Free Trader in Illinois ran it as "Perils of Miscegenation" and observed that couples who married across the color line in the South were "pretty certain to be brought before Judge Lynch and punished without ceremony or mercy". The Memphis Public Ledger headed it "Murder as a Purifier of a Stained Family Record", calling the shooting murder while repeating the family's motive.

The Chicago Tribune's version, reprinted in the Keowee Courier of Pickens Court House, the only South Carolina paper in the coverage, played the episode for laughs as "one of the most exciting honeymoons on record". It called Law "the dusky person who had with such bad taste forced himself into their family" and said that at last accounts "the negro was dying". Crime digests such as the "Tragical Tales" column in Minnesota and Wisconsin weeklies shrank the story to two sentences in which the brothers "killed the dusky bridegroom".

The papers disagree on whether Law died: a Columbia dispatch of October 29 and the briefs drawn from it said he "was killed", while the longer accounts called the wound mortal but said his death was not known. The longer accounts rest on the preacher, who had fled before he could learn the outcome, and no later report settled the question. The groom's name also varies: only the Ottawa printing gives "Manning Daw", while every other paper calls him Law.

reader.title: Shooting of Manning Law
bases: Two brothers of a white woman pursued her new Black husband and shot him, as reported, because of the marriage (A5, A6, A8), and the Ottawa Free Trader presented the case as one of 'Judge Lynch' (A7); it was a two-man pursuit, not a mob, and whether he died is disputed (A3, A6 vs. A8, A10).

Eight papers carried the story, but every version traces to Columbia or Charleston telegraph dispatches (A5, A6, A7) based on what the fleeing preacher told a correspondent (A5, A8); no South Carolina paper reported it first-hand, and the versions disagree on whether Law died (A6 vs. A8).

accounts.label: Columbia telegraph via the preacher (Times correspondent / Charleston special)
accounts.gist: Law, expecting death, fired first at Buck Creek; a return shot struck him in the breast with a wound that would 'probably prove mortal'; it was not known whether he died.

accounts.label: Columbia dispatch of October 29
accounts.gist: Law fired, the fire was returned and Law was killed; the preacher escaped to the woods and arrived in Columbia that morning.

accounts.label: 'Tragical Tales' crime-column brief
accounts.gist: The brothers pursued the couple and killed the bridegroom, then searched for the preacher, who escaped.

accounts.label: Chicago Tribune rewrite
accounts.gist: Facetious retelling: overtaken about ten miles out, Law shot in the breast; at last accounts he was dying and the brothers were reloading.

framing.detail: The Ottawa Free Trader said popular opinion against 'miscegenation' brought such couples 'before Judge Lynch' to be 'punished without ceremony or mercy', stating this as a fact about the South without approving or condemning it.
The Memphis Public Ledger headline called the shooting 'Murder as a Purifier of a Stained Family Record', naming it murder while echoing the family's motive.

The Chicago Tribune version, reprinted in the South Carolina Keowee Courier, mocked the victim as 'the dusky person who had with such bad taste forced himself into their family' and treated the shooting as a joke.
Digests and crime columns (Richmond Dispatch, Stephens City Star, 'Tragical Tales') printed short factual items, the latter calling Law 'the dusky bridegroom'.

versions.value: Fatally or mortally wounded, not known whether he died / 'dying' at last accounts

conflicts.note: The fuller dispatches, sourced to the preacher, who left the scene, say his death was not known; the shorter Oct. 29 dispatch and the brief derived from it say he was killed. Neither side reports a later confirmation.
Only the Ottawa printing has 'Daw', and its continuation calls the wounded man 'Lewis' (A8); 'Law' is the reading in every other paper.

versions.value: 'This morning' in a dispatch dated Oct. 28

conflicts.note: The Ottawa dispatch dated Oct. 28 also says the preacher reached Columbia 'last night' (A8), which does not fit a marriage that morning, so its dateline may be off by a day.
Not necessarily inconsistent; the Tribune rewrite gives only a distance.

record_check.dossier: One victim, Manning Law ('Daw' appears only in the Ottawa printing); the preacher who performed the marriage was also shot at.
Black ('a colored man', 'a cold, black negro man').
About October 27-28, 1881 (dispatch dated Oct. 28 says 'this morning'; others 'Friday' or 'Thursday last').
Two brothers of Mary Lewis ('the Lewis brothers'), not a mob.
No crime alleged; motive was his marriage to a white woman.
In pursuit: overtaken on the road while traveling by buggy.
Disputed: killed (A6, A3) vs. mortally wounded with death not known (A5, A8, A10).

record_check.record: Daw drew a pistol and fired at his pursuers; the account breaks off there.
record_check.dossier: The account continues: fire returned, Law shot in the breast, preacher chased; the groom is called Law in all but one paper.
Eight distinct white-press items (plus two reprints); known article sn85025431/1881-11-02/p1/a18 is a church notice, the brief is a100018.

info: Late October 1881: the marriage and pursuit took place 'this morning' per a Columbia telegraph dated October 28 (A7), on 'Friday' (A5, A10) or 'on Thursday last' (A1).
The couple were overtaken on the road toward Augusta, Ga., 'at a point called Buck Creek' (A5, A7), 'about ten miles on their journey' (A10).

Manning Law, described as 'a colored man' (A1, A9) and 'a cold, black negro man' (A5); named 'Manning Daw' in one version (A7) and plain 'Law' in others (A3, A6). A preacher, unnamed, who had performed the marriage was chased and shot at (A5, A8, A9).
No crime was alleged; the reported motive was his marriage to Mary Lewis, a white woman described as 'well connected' (A6) and of 'a respectable family' (A9).
The two brothers of Mary Lewis, called 'the Lewis brothers' (A5, A8, A9); not named individually.

Disputed: 'Law was killed' (A6) and 'killed the dusky bridegroom' (A3) vs. a wound that 'will probably prove fatal' or 'mortal', with 'not known whether the negro died' (A5, A8) and 'the negro was dying' at last accounts (A10); 'fatally wounded' (A1, A9).
The preacher hid in a thicket, escaped and reached Columbia by the night train (A8, A6); what became of Law's wife and her brothers was not known (A8).
